newsitem.title: USA: Despite gains, Asia still bars US investors-report.
newsitem.headline: Despite gains, Asia still bars US investors-report.

text.p: Asia's developing countries are lowering barriers to foreign access of securities firms and investors, but are still denying them national treatment and market access, an industry report issued Tuesday said.

The report by the Securities Industry Association was prepared in advance of financial service negotiations expected to begin in March under auspices of the World Trade Organization (WTO) and was sent to U.S. trade negotiators and other officials.

"While Asia's economic expansion has been complemented by a gradual reduction in barriers to foreign access, our study illustrates that U.S. securities firms and their clients still face fundamental denials of national treatment and market access," SIA Senior Vice President Steve Judge said in a letter to Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin that accompanied the study.

Restrictions include limits or bars to U.S. securities firms establishing wholly owned operations in the countries, ceilings on investment, restrictions on the introduction of new products, strict foreign exchange controls and lack of ability to comment on or review new regulations, the SIA said.

Since Washington failed to conclude a financial services agreement under the WTO in 1995, the SIA this year is urging U.S. negotiators to press for a deal that ends restrictions on foreign exchange dealings, inflows and outflows of capital and establishing a presence in the countries, Strongin said. The SIA will also seek to have U.S. firms treated under the same rules in Asian countries as domestic firms, he added.
U.S. investors' foreign holdings are projected to grow to $1 trillion by 2001 from about $500 billion now, he said.

Judge said rapidly developing Asian nations would benefit from freer trade in financial services by having greater access to the liquidity of U.S. markets and more efficient markets that would reduce the cost of their capital.
"Asia is critically imnportant," said Judge. "It's where there is tremendous opportunity."
SIA officials said they plan to study the financial service trading practices of countries in other parts of the world.

For example, China, which along with Malaysia, was seen as the most resgtrictive Asian country, excludes foreigners from owning "A" shares, according to the report's authors, David Strongin and Kristin Hofeditz.
Asian countries with the fewest restrictions on foreign investors and securities firms were Hong Kong and Singapore, they said.
Other countries studied in the report were India Indonesia, South Korea, the Philippines, Taiwan and Thailand.
"They all tend to discriminate in a number of ways," said Strongin.
